title: Root Ridge Leverage Score Sampling for ℓ Subspace Approximation
authors: David Woodruff (Carnegie Mellon University, PA), Taisuke Yasuda (The Voleon Group, NY)
abstract: The ℓ_p subspace approximation problem is an NP-hard low rank approximation problem that generalizes the median hyperplane problem ($p = 1$), principal component analysis ($p = 2$), and the center hyperplane problem ($p = \infty$). A popular approach to cope with the NP-hardness of this problem is to compute a \emph{strong coreset}, which is a small weighted subset of the input points which simultaneously approximates the cost of every k-dimensional subspace, typically to $(1+\varepsilon)$ relative error for a small constant $\varepsilon$. We obtain an algorithm for constructing a strong coreset for ℓ_p subspace approximation of size $\tilde O(k\varepsilon^{-4/p})$ for $p<2$ and $\tilde O(k^{p/2}\varepsilon^{-p})$ for $p>2$. This offers the following improvements over prior work: (1) we construct the first strong coresets with nearly optimal dependence on k for all $p\neq 2$. In prior work, \cite{SW2018} constructed coresets of modified points with a similar dependence on k, while \cite{HV2020} constructed true coresets with polynomially worse dependence on k, and (2) we recover or improve the best known $\varepsilon$ dependence for all $p$. In particular, for $p > 2$, the \cite{SW2018} coreset of modified points had a dependence of $\varepsilon^{-p^2/2}$ and the \cite{HV2020} coreset had a dependence of $\varepsilon^{-3p}$. Our algorithm is based on sampling by root ridge leverage scores, which admits fast algorithms, especially for sparse or structured matrices. Our analysis completely avoids the use of the representative subspace theorem \cite{SW2018}, which is a critical component of all prior dimension-independent coresets for ℓ_p subspace approximation. Our techniques also lead to the first nearly optimal \emph{online} strong coresets for ℓ_p subspace approximation with similar bounds as the offline setting, resolving a problem of \cite{WY2023b}. All prior approaches lose $\mathrm{poly}(k)$ factors in this setting, even when allowed to modify the original points.

A. The ℓp subspace approximation problem

these n points to lie on a low-dimensional subspace F ⊆ Rd
of rank k. This is an old and important question that has
been studied independently in varied fields such as operations
research, statistics, and computational geometry.

The flexibility of allowing for arbitrary values of p is also
crucial for tuning the behavior of the optimization problem to a
specific input distribution. As a toy example, consider an input
matrix A = B+G, where B is a n×n diagonal matrix with k
ones and n − k zeros on the diagonal, and G is i.i.d. Gaussian
noise with variance σ 2 . Then, the (p, 2)-norm of G to the power
p is roughly np/2+1 σ p while the (p, 2)-norm of A to the power
p is k((1 + σ)2 + (n − 1)σ 2 )p/2 + (n − k)np/2 σ p , that is, larger
by roughly an additive k. Thus, in order for the ℓp subspace
approximation problem to output a good approximation to B,
p must be tuned such that k = Ω(np/2+1 σ p ); otherwise, the 0
matrix is already a constant factor approximation. We stress
that any setting of p could be important here, depending on
the variance σ 2 of G. For instance, if σ 2 = k 2/3 /n5/3 , then
we should set p = 3, and if σ 2 = k 1/2 /n3/2 , then we should
set p = 4. Note that we also do not want to set p larger than
we have to, as we shall see that the complexity of the problem
increases for large p.

B. Sparsification and coresets
In big data settings, the number of points n is often
prohibitively large. Sparsification and coresets are a class of
techniques which have been extremely successful in handling
such parameter regimes. Sparsification generally refers to
the approximation of a large object by a sparse object, and
has been studied extensively in settings such as graphs [23]–
[25] and hypergraphs [26]–[29] as well as a large variety of
decomposable loss functions such as clustering [2], [30]–[38],
submodular functions [39], [40], ℓp regression [41]–[45], and
generalized linear models [46]–[49]. When the object being
sparsified is a dataset, then its sparse approximation is often
called a coreset. Coresets can often be used as a substantially
smaller drop-in replacement of the original dataset, and leads
to both time- and space-efficient algorithms.

I-B1, strong coresets that use an additional coordinate as in [1],

The literature of online algorithms studies algorithms which
must make irrevocable decisions as its input arrives incrementally. In online machine learning and data analysis, a
typical setting is for new data points to arrive one by one. The
algorithm must then immediately make a decision about this
data point, such as assigning them to clusters [74] or outputting
a prediction [75]. The online coreset model, introduced by work
of [76], studies the question of implementing coreset algorithms
in such online settings. More specifically, the rows of our design
matrix A ∈ Rn×d arrive one by one in a stream, and we must
sample the rows of the coreset in an online fashion, that is,
we must decide whether or not to keep a row i ∈ [n] when it
arrives, and we cannot discard rows that we keep, or retrieve
rows that we discard. This model was originally studied in
the context of coresets for ℓ2 linear regression [76], and has
subsequently been analyzed for a variety of problems in data
analysis, computational geometry, and numerical linear algebra
[3], [45], [62], [63], [77], [78].

Question I.5. Are there online coreset algorithms for constructing strong coresets for ℓp subspace approximation of size
Õ(k) poly(ε−1 ) for p < 2 and Õ(k p/2 ) poly(ε−1 ) for p > 2?
In the online coreset setting, all prior techniques for
dimension-free coresets [1], [2], [58] face a key challenge.
The problem is that all of these techniques are based on
computing a fixed low-dimensional subspace S which is used
to construct the coreset. In the online coreset setting, this is
a major obstruction, due to the fact that this low-dimensional
subspace S can evolve as more inputs arrive. In the recent work
of [3], it was shown that this problem can be circumvented by
bounding the number of times that a subspace can undergo a
significant change, using the so-called online Lewis weights
[45]. However, this technique increases the coreset size by
the number of times this subspace changes, which is a factor
of Õ(k max{1,p/2} ), leading to a suboptimal overall bound of
Õ(k p+O(1) ) poly(ε−1 ). In particular, the extra factor of k p/2 is
a glaring gap in our understanding of this problem, as pointed
out by [3].
Despite these challenges, our work gives a positive resolution
of Question I.5 by introducing a completely new approach
towards coresets for ℓp subspace approximation. One of the key
aspects of our techniques will be to avoid a “commitment” to a
specific low dimensional subspace via the use of regularization,
and will allow us to seamlessly handle the online coreset setting.

E. Corollaries
1) Streaming algorithms: A simple corollary of our nearly
optimal constructions for strong coresets is that we immediately
obtain similar results in streaming model of computation. In the
streaming model, the rows ai of the input matrix A arrive one
at a time, and we wish to maintain a strong coreset for A. In
this setting, the classic merge-and-reduce technique (see, e.g.,
[63] for a discussion) shows that a construction for a coreset
of size Õ(k c ) poly(ε−1 ) can be converted into a streaming
implementation of size Õ(k c ) poly(ε−1 log n) by setting the
accuracy parameter to ε′ = ε/ log n and composing the coreset
construction in a binary tree fashion. Recent work of [66] shows
that this argument can in fact be sharpened to a poly(log log n)
factor overhead rather than poly(log n), by first computing an
online coreset (see Section I-C1), as we show in Section IV-B.
2) Entrywise ℓp low rank approximation: For p < 2, our
nearly optimal coresets for ℓp subspace approximation imply
new algorithms for the related problem of entrywise ℓp low
rank approximation.
